label: Robotics and Theorem Proving
notes: This chapter spans printed pages 297 through 350 and showcases two striking applications. Robot kinematics and automatic geometric theorem proving both reduce to polynomial systems, so Grobner bases and elimination become practical engines for motion planning and for mechanically verifying classical theorems of Euclidean geometry.

label: Forward Kinematics
notes: A robot arm is modeled as linked segments with revolute or prismatic joints. The forward kinematics problem expresses the position and orientation of the hand as polynomial functions of the joint parameters, using trigonometric identities recast as polynomial relations between sines and cosines on the unit circle.

label: Inverse Kinematics
notes: The inverse kinematics problem asks which joint settings achieve a desired hand position, that is, to solve the kinematic equations for the joint variables. Elimination theory and Grobner bases reduce this nonlinear system, revealing the configuration space and the number of distinct solutions for a given target.

label: Configuration Space
notes: The set of all achievable configurations forms a variety in the joint parameters, whose geometry controls reachability and singularities. Studying this configuration space with the algebraic tools developed earlier exposes where the robot loses degrees of freedom and which targets lie outside its workspace.

label: Geometry as Polynomials
notes: Automatic theorem proving translates a Euclidean configuration into coordinates, turning hypotheses and the conclusion into polynomial equations. A theorem holds when the conclusion polynomial vanishes on the variety of the hypotheses, a condition tested by ideal membership or by computing a remainder.

label: Proving Theorems Mechanically
notes: The conclusion follows from the hypotheses, possibly after excluding degenerate cases, exactly when it lies in the radical of the hypothesis ideal, checked by the Nullstellensatz and Grobner bases. Classical results like the theorem of Apollonius fall out automatically. Next: invariant theory of finite groups.
